title: Blowing cosmic bubbles
caption: Wisps of the bubble Sh2-308 around EZ Canis Majoris, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: EZ Canis Majoris, Sh2-308 · constellation Canis Major · about 5000 light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: A few fine threads of gas stretch across this Hubble view. They are part of Sh2-308, a faint, wispy shell in Canis Major, the Great Dog, some 5200 light-years away. The shell wraps around a single star, EZ Canis Majoris.

That star is a Wolf-Rayet star, a hugely bright type that is tens of times more massive than the Sun and sits at the extreme end of stellar evolution. The ancestors of such stars shed thick winds that stripped away their outer layers. The fierce, fast wind of the Wolf-Rayet star then sweeps up the surrounding material into bubbles.

EZ Canis Majoris cast off its own outer layers to make these strands, and its intense radiation keeps pushing the bubble outward. Its edges are now about 60 light-years apart. Such bubbles do not last, because the stars that inflate them will eventually explode as supernovae and swallow them.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (2.66 x 2.72 arcminutes) and distance (5000 light years), the frame spans roughly 3.9 × 4 light-years. Its light set out about 5,000 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 imaged the gas through narrow filters that isolate light from oxygen and nitrogen. The source does not publish which color was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: The shell is described as faint and tenuous, far too dim for the eye. Hubble's narrow filters and long exposures pick out the glow of specific gases.

behind.exposure: Not published on the source page.
behind.technique: Not stated by the source (single frame, stack, mosaic or panorama unknown).

explore: Wolf-Rayet stars rank with the most luminous and heaviest stars in the Universe. Hubble captured only a few of the tenuous threads that make up the shell.
alt: Thin, wispy threads of glowing gas from a faint bubble around a massive star.
